name: Hydra sequencer
description: Pick up the next queued issue anywhere in the organisation, take a slot and a per-issue lock, gate it, advance its label, release. This is what replaces hydra-supervisor.sh's poll loop — see openspec/changes/hydra-flows-first-port tasks 3.1 and 3.2 and builder-write-access-hardening task 0.

$bindings.find-work.source: The uuid of the Source seeded from flows/hydra-forge.source.json on the target instance. Instance-specific; an importer resolves it by name.
$bindings.describe-repo.source: The uuid of the Source seeded from flows/hydra-forge.source.json on the target instance. Instance-specific; an importer resolves it by name.
$bindings.advance.source: The uuid of the Source seeded from flows/hydra-forge.source.json on the target instance. Instance-specific; an importer resolves it by name.
$bindings.advance-failed.source: The uuid of the Source seeded from flows/hydra-forge.source.json on the target instance. Instance-specific; an importer resolves it by name.
$bindings.run-stage.credentialId: A DISTINCT credential from the Source uuids above — NOT the same one, which is what this entry used to say. The forge Source uses provider `github`, a host-locked PROXY whose `resolveInjectable()` returns null BY DESIGN so the secret never leaves OpenRegister. `run-stage` cannot use that: the ExApp fetches a tool tree and pushes, and git speaks the smart-HTTP pack protocol, so there is no single request for the broker to make on its behalf. It needs provider `github-push` (`inject_only: true`), whose secret is handed to the sidecar behind GIT_ASKPASS. A proxy credential cannot be injected and an inject-only credential cannot be proxied, so binding both references to one uuid fails whichever credential it names. ⚠️ The push credential MUST be a FINE-GRAINED token scoped to ONE repository with `Contents: Read and write` and NOT `Workflows` — see the requirements on the `github-push` entry in openregister's credential-providers.json, including the workflow-probe that must be refused before the token is stored. It is NOT a placeholder: a credential id is instance-specific, so it cannot be checked in, and it is not derivable from anything the tick carries. Leaving it as `{{forgeCredential}}` is what sent the LITERAL STRING `{{forgeCredential}}` to the broker, which answered `credential not found` — a message that reads as a missing credential rather than an unrendered placeholder (openregister#2245). See hydra#537.
$bindings.run-build.pushCredentialId: The `github-push` (inject_only) credential. Instance-specific. Without it the stage falls back to the proxy credential, which cannot be injected, and the build fails at the push having done all its work.
$bindings.run-build.llmCredentialId: The `anthropic-cli` (inject_only) credential. Instance-specific. Without it the command runs with no model token and `claude` reports "Not logged in".

$comment: 🔑 THE FLOW IS THE AUTHORITY ON WHAT RUNS NEXT (task 3.2). No stage chooses its
own successor and no daemon polls: a scheduled tick reads the queue, decides,
and moves the label. `hydra-supervisor.sh` is a 3,937-line loop doing this.
The two guarantees it enforces are DIFFERENT and are enforced differently:
claim-slot  at most N concurrent — a resource cap. Brief overshoot costs CPU
and corrupts nothing, so a single-step claim on flow state is
enough (openregister#2221), made safe by a scheduled flow never
overlapping itself (openregister#2218).
lock-issue  ONE run per issue — this must be EXACT. Two stages on one issue
duplicate commits and drive the label state machine from two
places. Enforced by IDENTITY: an object write with
`onConflict: fail`, where the DATABASE arbitrates.
The lock was re-measured through the node on 2026-07-31 rather than trusted:
twelve simultaneous runs claiming one identifier gave 1 completed / 11 stopped,
each loser told `already exists`, and exactly one row. `tasks.md` recorded
per-issue locking as having 'no node equivalent' — that was true when written
and stopped being true at openregister#2215.
🔑 THIS FLOW IS NOW SCHEDULE-SAFE (builder-write-access-hardening task 0.4).
The previous revision said, correctly, that it was not: `{{repo}}`,
`{{queueLabel}}`, `{{runLabel}}`, `{{failLabel}}`, `{{lockId}}`, `{{branch}}`
and `{{forgeCredential}}` were all caller-supplied and a schedule tick
supplies NONE of them. The reaper's fix (task 0) asked one question of each
of its own placeholders — is this genuinely input, or can the flow derive
it? — and the same question, asked here, has three different answers:
DERIVED FROM THE WORK   `repo`, `issueNumber`, the lock id (as `repoSlug`
plus `issueNumber`) and the stage ref. The sequencer searches the whole
organisation, so the repository arrives WITH the issue rather than
before it, and everything about the issue follows from the issue.
CONSTANT                the three labels and the lock marker. These are
hydra conventions, not per-run values, and both halves of every one of
them live in this repository — so they are hardcoded at both ends the
way the reaper's `name` marker is, not left for an importer. A reader
pointed at a different string from the writer is indistinguishable from
a reader that found nothing to do.
BOUND                   the Source uuid and the forge credential uuid.
These are the only two values that are genuinely neither derivable nor
constant: they identify objects on a particular instance. `$bindings`
already existed for exactly this and now covers both.
What is left is a graph in which every value is a literal, a computation over
inputs the engine always has, or something read off a forge response — and
the only remaining placeholder a CALLER may fill, `branch`, is an override
applied through `coalesce`, which always yields a value. A manual or
event-triggered run may still seed `org` or `branch`; neither is required,
and that path is deliberately preserved rather than closed.
⚠️ STILL `enabled: false`, AND THE REASON HAS CHANGED — read this before
flipping it. The old reason was technical and is gone: the flow could not
fire, and now it can (proved by firing it from `FlowScheduleWorker` with no
caller input). The remaining reason is operational. Unlike the reaper, which
only deletes hydra's own stale locks, an enabled sequencer MUTATES REAL
REPOSITORIES every five minutes: it applies `build:pass` / `build:fail` to
live issues and dispatches gate runs that take up to 25 minutes each. That
is a deployment decision with a blast radius, not a bug fix, so it is left
to whoever operates the instance rather than switched on inside the change
that made it possible.
⚠️ The lock is taken and never released by this graph. Releasing it belongs
with stage completion, which is not built yet. Reaping an ABANDONED one is
`hydra-lock-reaper.flow.json`, and as of builder-write-access-hardening
task 0 that reaper is enabled and demonstrably fires on its own schedule.
Its filter is the constant `name` this flow writes plus `@self.created`, so
the two halves agree by a literal rather than by intention — change the
literal in one place and `test-flow-definitions.sh` fails.
⚠️ CONSEQUENTLY A SECOND TICK ON THE SAME ISSUE IS REFUSED, not skipped. The
flow does not mark the issue `build:running` before gating, so five minutes
later the search still returns it. `lock-issue` is what stops the duplicate:
the second run stops at `already exists` and never reaches the forge. That
is the designed behaviour and it was measured rather than assumed — but it
means a wedged lock stalls that issue until the reaper's cutoff, which is
precisely why the reaper had to work first.

config.$comment: The search the tick is about to run, ASSEMBLED rather than received. A schedule tick's payload is only `{flowId, scheduledAt}`, so every value this flow needs has to be a constant, a computation, or something derived from what it finds — never something a caller happens to pass. The organisation is the one genuine piece of configuration in the whole graph and it is applied through `coalesce`, which always yields a value: an operator running a fork can seed `org`, and a tick that seeds nothing still gets `ConductionNL`. The queue label is a CONSTANT, written here exactly once, for the same reason the lock marker is a constant — see the note on `advance`.

🔑 THE SEQUENCER POLLS THE ORGANISATION, NOT A REPOSITORY. This used to be `GET /repos/{{repo}}/issues`, and `repo` is exactly the value a schedule tick cannot supply — it rendered empty, the call went to `/repos//issues`, and GitHub answered `404 Not Found`. Threading a repository in from somewhere would have been the wrong fix twice over. First, a repository is not an input to 'what should the pipeline do next' — it is a PROPERTY OF THE WORK, and `derive` below reads it back off the issue that was found. Second, there is no list to thread: `_forgejo_work_list_repos` was deleted with `hydra-supervisor.sh` (#466) and nothing replaced it. The supervisor had already learned this lesson the expensive way — it moved from per-repo enumeration to ONE org-wide search because 41 repos x 5 label queries = 205 calls per tick got the runner's IP flagged as abusive by Codeberg's WAF. `/search/issues` is GitHub's equivalent of the `/repos/issues/search` endpoint it settled on. Measured on 2026-08-02: `org:ConductionNL is:issue is:open label:"build:queued"` returns 4 open issues across several repositories in a single call. NOTE that the endpoint now carries NO placeholder at all. That is the property worth keeping — `FlowConfigGuard::assertEndpointContained()` re-checks the RENDERED endpoint, but only for escape (absolute URL, traversal); `/repos//issues` is relative and traversal-free, so the guard passed it and GitHub was the thing that said no.

`/search/issues` wraps its results in `items` alongside `total_count`, where `/repos/{repo}/issues` returned a bare array. So the emptiness test is on `queue.body.items`, not on `queue.body`. Getting this wrong fails in the worst direction: `length` of a non-array is its STRING length, so testing the wrapper object would be non-empty on every tick and the work branch would be taken with nothing in hand.

🔑 THE REPOSITORY IS READ BACK OFF THE WORK, which is what lets the search be org-wide. A search result carries `repository_url` — an absolute API URL like `https://api.github.com/repos/ConductionNL/openregister` — and NOT a `repository` object and NOT a `full_name`, so the owner/name pair has to be recovered by stripping the prefix. Verified against the live API rather than assumed: the item keys are `repository_url`, `number`, `labels`, … with no `repository` member. 🔑 `lockId` IS DERIVED, NOT SUPPLIED, and that is a CORRECTNESS requirement rather than a schedule-tick convenience. The lock's entire job is that two runs which pick the same issue collide on it — `onConflict: fail` makes the DATABASE arbitrate. A caller-supplied identifier defeats that by construction: two ticks passing two different ids both succeed, the mutual exclusion the lock exists for is gone, and every run still reports success. So the id is a pure function of the thing being locked. `repoSlug` exists only because the id must survive being an identifier: `ConductionNL/openregister` carries a slash.  🔑 THE SPEC IS CARRIED, NOT REDISCOVERED. hydra is spec-driven: an issue is always about an OpenSpec change, that change is a folder in the target repo, and `hydra.json` sits beside it as the record. The change slug is in the issue body — `openspec/changes/<slug>/` — and nothing used to read it, so a stage ran without knowing which spec it was implementing and the recorder had no path to write to. Derived by SPLIT because the expression language has no regex: the operators are upper/lower/trim/split/join/replace/now. `compute` keys chain (applyCompute assigns per key, in order), so each line reads the one above. Verified against all four issues queued at the time of writing: validate-self-folder-access, milestone-tracking, method-decomposition, document-zaakdossier — 4 of 4.  The three `change*` scratch keys stay on the item deliberately: `set-fields` applies remove → rename → set → compute, so a key computed here cannot be removed here, and a second node purely to tidy them would cost a transition for cosmetics. Verified end-to-end against the LIVE engine rather than reasoned about — a probe flow returned change=`validate-self-folder-access` and recordPath=`openspec/changes/validate-self-folder-access/hydra.json`, which is what proves `split`, `var` array-indexing and per-key chaining all behave as written. 
🔑 THE SLUG IS TERMINATED EXPLICITLY, AND THE `/` SPLIT IS NOT ENOUGH.
`changeBits` splits on `/` and takes element 0, which is right only when
the slug is followed by another path segment. It usually is not — an issue
body writes `openspec/changes/p2-meeting-management` and then keeps
talking, so with no `/` to stop at, element 0 is the slug PLUS everything
after it. Measured on planix#248, `change` came out as:

    p2-meeting-management`  <newline> <newline> Queued for Hydra build (placement

which reached `read-change` as an endpoint containing a CONTROL CHARACTER.
`FlowConfigGuard::assertEndpointContained()` refused it before any request,
and the run died there.

⚠️ `onError: continue` DID NOT COVER IT, and that distinction is worth
keeping: the refusal happened while the endpoint was being RENDERED, not
as an HTTP failure, so the error policy never applied. An error policy
protects the CALL; it does not protect the ARGUMENTS.

The expression language has `split`, `join`, `replace`, `trim` and NO
regex, so termination is a chain of splits — one per character that can
legitimately follow a slug in prose. Each step takes element 0, so a slug
already terminated by an earlier separator passes through the rest
untouched.

⚠️ THE KEY ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING. `applyCompute()` assigns per key in
sequence, so every `…Parts` must be written before the `…Cut` that reads
it. Written in the other order the whole chain silently yields empty, and
an empty slug builds the endpoint `/contents/openspec/changes/` — which is
a real directory, answers 200, and would send every unspecced issue
straight through the gate this feeds.

An issue with no OpenSpec change is REFUSED rather than built. hydra is spec-driven — the change is what the work is about, and `hydra.json` beside it is where the result is recorded — so a stage with no spec has nowhere to write and nothing to be judged against. Same shape as `refuse-unattributed` in hydra-record-stage: refuse loudly rather than proceed with a hole. This rejects none of the queue it was written against (4 of 4 carry a change folder); it exists so the FIFTH one that does not is visible instead of silent.

🔴 THIS DEFAULT NAMED `refuse-unspecced` — THE END NODE — AND THAT MADE THE
REFUSAL A LOOP. When the refusal path grew a body (`flag-unspecced` →
`dequeue-unspecced` → `refuse-unspecced`), `spec-exists-gate`'s default was
moved to the new head and this one was not. The EDGE was added here; only
the route target was missed, so the graph looked wired and the router still
jumped straight to the terminal.

An issue naming no change therefore ended the run WITHOUT being labelled and
WITHOUT leaving the queue — and `find-work` searches on `build:queued`, so
the next tick five minutes later selected the same issue and refused it
again, forever. `dequeue-unspecced`'s own comment describes exactly this
('it is not a refusal — it is a loop') for the sibling path.

⚠️ IT IS INVISIBLE FROM THE RUN LOG, which is why it survived. Every tick
reports `completed`, and `flag-unspecced` logs `in 0 out 0` — a heartbeat,
indistinguishable from the normal case where the issue DID name a change and
simply took the other exit. Nothing anywhere prints 'this issue has now been
refused eleven times'.

🔴🔥 AND POINTING IT AT `flag-unspecced` — THE OBVIOUS FIX — DID NOT WORK.
Measured with an issue that names no change (openregister#2469):

    spec-gate         in 1 out 1   item tagged `flag-unspecced`
    spec-exists-gate  in 0 out 0   heartbeat
    flag-unspecced    in 0 out 0   nothing arrived

Same loss as `build-blocked`: `advanceItems()` ASSIGNS to a firing node's
output places whether or not it produced items, so `spec-exists-gate`'s empty
firing overwrote the place `spec-gate` had just filled. The issue kept
`build:queued`, and the run reported `completed`. The loop was still a loop —
the fix had simply moved where it was invisible.

🔑 SO THIS DEFAULT GETS ITS OWN CHAIN: `flag-nospec` → `dequeue-nospec` →
`refuse-unspecced`. Two nodes duplicated rather than one place shared. The
end node is shared safely because an END consumes no items.

🔑 A MENTION IS NOT AN EXISTENCE PROOF. `spec-gate` above only asks
whether the issue BODY contains `openspec/changes/`, which `derive` then
splits a slug out of. That says the author typed a path; it says nothing
about whether the path is there.

Measured across the queue this pipeline actually serves:

    planix/openspec/changes/        404 — the directory is absent ENTIRELY
    procest/openspec/changes/       only `archive`
    openregister .../register-resolver-service   404 on main AND development

So the gate passed issue after issue whose spec was never committed, took
a slot and a lock for each, cloned the repository, spent twenty minutes of
model time, and handed the agent an empty proposal — which it then
correctly declined to build. Every one of those runs was decided before
the first byte was cloned; this is where that decision belongs.

🔴 IT NOW ASKS ABOUT `stageRef`, AND THE COMMENT THAT USED TO SIT HERE WAS
RIGHT WHEN IT WAS WRITTEN AND WRONG BY THE TIME IT MATTERED. It argued that
omitting `?ref=` was deliberate, because the contents endpoint defaults to
the repository's DEFAULT branch and that is 'exactly what `resolve-ref` will
pick for `stageRef` further down'.

That premise was removed by hydra#561. `resolve-ref` now prefers
`development` over the declared default, because this fleet develops there
and `main` is whatever was last released. So the two diverged: this node
asked `main` while the build targeted `development`.

⚠️ AND THE FAILURE IS A SILENT, CORRECT-LOOKING REFUSAL. A change committed
on `development` but not on `main` answers 404 here, `spec-exists-gate`
routes it to `flag-unspecced`, and the issue is labelled `build:blocked` and
dequeued — 'this issue names a change that is not in the repository', which
is a sentence about a change that IS in the repository. openregister's
default branch is `main`, so it is squarely exposed. Nothing errors; the run
reports `completed`.

🔑 SO `describe-repo` / `read-dev-ref` / `resolve-ref` MOVED IN FRONT OF
THIS NODE. They are three read-only lookups that need no slot and no lock,
so running them earlier costs nothing and gives this check the branch the
build will actually use. The original ordering existed to keep the refusal
cheap; it still is — the refusal happens before `claim-slot`, exactly as
before.

⚠️ `onError: continue`, because a 404 IS THE ANSWER this node exists to
get. Stopping on it would turn the refusal into a crashed run, and a
crashed run leaves the issue queued for the next tick to crash on again.

Routes on the STATUS, and requires it to be exactly 200.

⚠️ MEASURED, because the shape is not what it looks like. Under
`onError: continue` a 404 does NOT arrive as `{status: 404}` — the node
emits an `__error` record and `changeDir.status` is absent entirely. So
this condition succeeds on a present spec (`http=200`, body/headers/
callLog) and falls through on an absent one because the path resolves to
null, not because it resolves to 404.

That is why the test is `=== 200` and not `!== 404`: the second would
read a MISSING status as a pass and admit every issue whose spec lookup
failed for any reason at all — a rate limit, a network blip, a renamed
repository — which is the failure this gate exists to stop, arriving
through the one door left open.

Both directions proven against the live forge:
  planix/p2-meeting-management   absent  -> flag-unspecced, claim-slot got 0 items
  openregister/file-actions      http=200 -> claim-slot

🔑 The second half of that is the half worth running. A gate that refuses
EVERYTHING passes the refusal test perfectly.

The issue is refused, and SAYS SO ON ITSELF. Both refusals arrive here —
an issue naming no change at all, and one naming a change that is not in
the repository — because from a reader's point of view they are the same
problem: there is nothing to build against.

⚠️ `build:blocked` is new vocabulary, like `build:no-change`, and
`scripts/create-labels.sh` creates neither. GitHub auto-creates a label on
first use, which is how this fleet already carries a grey undescribed
`build:fail` beside a curated `build:failed`.

🔑 THE REFUSAL PATH MUST LEAVE THE QUEUE TOO, OR IT IS NOT A REFUSAL — it
is a loop. `refuse-unspecced` ended the run and left `build:queued` in
place, and `find-work` searches on exactly that label with `per_page: 1`.
So the first unbuildable issue in the organisation became the permanent
head of the queue: every tick re-found it, refused it again, and dispatched
nothing else, forever.

That is the same defect #542 removed from the verdict path, in a second
place, and it was latent only because the three issues queued at the time
happened to name a change. It is hydra#543.

⚠️ Nothing is released here because nothing was taken: this path runs
BEFORE `claim-slot` and `lock-issue`. That ordering is the point — a
refusal that had already spent a slot and a lock would need to unwind
them, and an unwind is one more thing to get wrong.

`flag-unspecced` for the OTHER refusal: an issue that names no OpenSpec
change at all, as opposed to one that names a change the repository does not
have. Same label, same meaning to a reader — hydra will not build this, go
and look at the issue.

🔴 IT IS A SEPARATE NODE BECAUSE SHARING ONE COST THE FIX ENTIRELY.
`spec-gate`'s default pointed at `flag-unspecced`, the edge was there, the
routing was correct — and the item never arrived, because
`FlowItemPlacement::advanceItems()` assigns to a firing node's output places
even when that firing produced nothing, and `spec-exists-gate` fires as a
heartbeat between `spec-gate` and the consumer. Measured on
openregister#2469: `spec-gate in 1 out 1`, `flag-unspecced in 0 out 0`, issue
still `build:queued`, run `completed`.

🔑 THE SAME SHAPE AS `build-blocked` / `verdict-blocked`. The rule that keeps
coming out of this engine: two branches of one pass must not write the same
place. Duplicating a four-line source-call is the cheap side of that trade.

`dequeue-unspecced` for the no-change-named branch, and it exists for the
same reason `flag-nospec` does: the branch needs a chain nobody else writes
to. Sharing `dequeue-unspecced` would put the identical wipe one node
further along.

🔑 WITHOUT THIS THE REFUSAL IS A LOOP, which is the whole point of the
sibling path: `find-work` searches on `build:queued` with `per_page: 1`, so
an issue that is refused but never dequeued becomes the permanent head of
the queue and starves every other issue in the organisation.

⚠️ Nothing is released here because nothing was taken — this runs BEFORE
`claim-slot` and `lock-issue`.

`holder` and `record` name `repo`, which `derive` has just computed. They were reaching for a caller-supplied value before, so on a tick the pool was keyed on the empty string and every repository contended for one holder's worth of slots. 
🔑 THE LEASE IS WHAT STOPS A LOST SLOT BEING A PERMANENT ONE. Every node
between here and `release` can end the run — `lock-issue` carries
`onError: stop`, and a build or a fix can outlive its deadline. Each of
those leaves a slot held by a run that no longer exists, and nothing
reaps slots. Measured: one such run held a slot for four hours while the
other two sat free; three of them and this repository could never be
built again.

⚠️ AND IT WOULD NOT LOOK BROKEN. A full pool routes to `stop-full`, which
is a normal outcome — the flow reports `completed` every five minutes
while dispatching nothing.

5400 seconds is 90 minutes: comfortably longer than the worst honest run
this graph can have (a 25-minute build, a 25-minute fix, two gate passes)
and short enough that a leak clears within the hour. Too SHORT is the
dangerous direction — it would displace a live builder and put two runs
on one issue — which is why it is set from the timeouts above it rather
than guessed.

🔑 `name` IS A CONSTANT, and that is the reaper's whole contract. `hydra-lock-reaper` runs on a schedule, and a schedule tick's payload is only `{flowId, scheduledAt}` — so a name carrying `{{repo}}` gave the reaper a filter it could never render, which is how the reaper spent weeks matching nothing and reporting `completed`. The marker that says 'this row is a lock' therefore has to be identical for every writer and free of interpolation; which issue it belongs to is DESCRIPTION, which nothing filters on. ⚠️ A previous revision also stamped an epoch into `notes` and the lockId into `description`, because `@self.created` range filters returned zero rows and a delete could not match on `uuid`. openregister#2269 and #2270 fixed both, and both hacks are gone: the age is `_created` again and the reaper's delete names the row by uuid. Do not reintroduce them — `notes` is the field the flow SEEDER writes provenance prose into, and a lexicographic range over it would compare epochs against English.

🔑 THE REF IS ASKED FOR, NOT GUESSED. `run-stage` needs a ref and `{{branch}}` was caller-supplied, so on a tick it rendered empty — and `HermiqWorkloadNode::assertConfigured()` cannot catch that, because it validates the AUTHORED config (`"{{branch}}"`, which is not empty) rather than the rendered value. A hardcoded default was the obvious alternative and it is measurably wrong: on 2026-08-02 `ConductionNL/hydra` and `ConductionNL/openregister` default to `main` while `ConductionNL/hermiq` defaults to `development`, so any single literal is wrong for a large part of the fleet — and wrong in the direction of gating a branch nobody develops on. The forge already knows the answer per repository, so this asks it. One extra call per tick, on the work branch only, is affordable in a way the 205-call fan-out this flow's search deliberately avoids is not.

🔑 THE DEFAULT BRANCH IS THE WRONG BRANCH FOR THIS FLEET, and building on
it wasted an entire run before anyone noticed.

`resolve-ref` used to take `repoInfo.body.default_branch`, which GitHub
reports as `main`. Every app here develops on `development`, and `main`
is whatever was last released — on openregister, measured today:

    development is 5309 commits ahead of main

So a build ran against a tree 5,309 commits stale. The agent read the
spec from it, wrote code against neighbours that had since changed, and
the gates judged the result using that tree's CONFIGURATION — which is
why gate-65 reported fourteen coding-standard deviations that were fixed
on `development` weeks ago:

    main         .php-cs-fixer.dist.php absent · .editorconfig absent
                 conduction/coding-standard ABSENT
    development  both present · conduction/coding-standard ^1.0

⚠️ EVERY LAYER OF THAT LOOKED FINE. The clone succeeded, the spec was
there (`file-actions` exists on both branches), the agent produced real
code, the gates ran and returned a real number. Nothing failed — the
whole run was simply about the wrong tree, and the only visible symptom
was a gate complaining about debt that no longer exists.

So this asks whether `development` exists rather than assuming it. A repo
without one keeps its default branch, which is what `resolve-ref`'s
`coalesce` falls back to — nothing is forced.

The branch everything downstream stands on: the agent builds from it, the
gates diff against it, and the pull request targets it.

🔑 THE ORDER IS THE POINT. A caller-supplied `branch` wins, because a
manual run may be aiming somewhere specific. Otherwise `development` when
the repository has one — this fleet's apps all develop there and `main` is
whatever was last released. Only then the repository's declared default,
for a repo that genuinely has no `development`.

⚠️ `devBranch` is computed from a STATUS, not from a truthy body. Under
`onError: continue` a 404 leaves `devRef.status` absent entirely, so
`=== 200` is the only test that distinguishes 'the branch is there' from
'the lookup did not answer' — and the second must fall through to the
default rather than build on a branch nobody confirmed exists.

⚠️ `devBranch` IS ASSIGNED BEFORE `stageRef`, AND THAT ORDER IS THE FIX.
`applyCompute()` walks the map in key order, so a `stageRef` still sitting
in its original position — written before `devBranch` existed — coalesced
past a null and resolved to `main` while `devBranch` held 'development' one
line later. Measured exactly that on the first attempt:

    devRef.status=200   devBranch='development'   ->   stageRef='main'

🔑 The same trap as the change-slug chain in `derive`, and it looked just as
correct: every value present, every value right, and the one that mattered
read a moment too early.

command:
Implement the OpenSpec change `{{change}}` in this repository, as asked for by issue #{{issueNumber}}: {{issueTitle}}

The change's own documents are in `openspec/changes/{{change}}/` — read `proposal.md`, `tasks.md`, `design.md` and anything under `specs/` before you write a line. You are in a real checkout of `{{repo}}` at branch `{{stageRef}}`, so read whatever else you need.

THE STAGE THAT WRITES CODE. Everything before this node finds work and locks it; everything after judges what came out. This is the only step that authors anything.

It runs `claude` IN THE CLONE, which is the whole difference from the agent-step transport: `hermiq.agent-step` has no shell, no filesystem and no checkout, so it can only be handed excerpts in a prompt and asked to return content — and a tree entry replaces a path wholesale, so a file it never saw is a file it deletes. Here it reads and edits the real thing.

🔑 `llmCredentialId` IS A THIRD CREDENTIAL and not a reuse of `credentialId`. That one is a host-locked PROXY entry spent server-side fetching the tool tree, and `resolveInjectable()` refuses that shape by design, so it cannot put anything in this container. The model token must be inject-only, and the runner hands it only to a command its own per-command allowlist names — a gates run in the same image receives nothing.

⚠️ THE AGENT IS TOLD NOT TO RUN GIT, and that instruction is a courtesy rather than the control. The runner withholds the forge credential from the command child precisely BECAUSE `push` is declared here, and performs the push itself afterwards behind `pushGuard`: the branch must match `feature/<issueNumber>/<slug>`, the remote must be the one declared, dependency manifests and forbidden prefixes are refused outright, and every changed path must fall inside `scope`. An agent that ignored the instruction would find no credential and no route.

🔑 `scope` IS A FENCE, NOT A HINT. An empty list would leave only the forbidden-prefix rules standing, so the paths a build may touch are named here: an implementation lives in `lib`, `src`, `tests`, `openspec` and `appinfo`, and a change that needs to move outside them is a change that needs a human.

⚠️ Gated on hermiq#209 — until that ships, `/stage` carries no credential channel and `claude` is not on the runner's command allowlist, so this node fails closed rather than running an unauthenticated CLI.

🔑 THREE CREDENTIALS, AND EACH ONE IS A DIFFERENT SHAPE THAT THE OTHER
TWO CANNOT SUBSTITUTE FOR. This node needs all three at once, which is
why they are three fields and not one:

  credentialId      `github`, a host-locked PROXY. Spent SERVER-SIDE by
                    the broker fetching the tool tarball.
                    `resolveInjectable()` returns null for it by
                    design, so it can put nothing in the container.
  pushCredentialId  `github-push`, `inject_only`. git speaks the
                    smart-HTTP pack protocol, so there is no single
                    request for the broker to make on its behalf — the
                    token has to be IN the container, behind GIT_ASKPASS.
  llmCredentialId   `anthropic-cli`, `inject_only`. A different VENDOR
                    entirely: the two above reach the forge, this one
                    lets the command answer.

⚠️ WITHOUT `pushCredentialId` THIS NODE FAILS AT THE PUSH AND NOWHERE
EARLIER. `StageDispatchService` falls back to `credentialId` when it is
absent — deliberately, so every read-only stage that predates the
parameter keeps working — and that fallback resolves to the PROXY, for
which `resolveInjectable()` correctly returns null. The stage then runs
the whole build, edits the tree, and finds no credential at the moment
it tries to push. Everything up to that point looks perfect.

⚠️ A CREDENTIAL ID IS INSTANCE-SPECIFIC AND CANNOT BE GUESSED. Both
uuids here were wrong on first writing: `llmCredentialId` was recorded
from memory as `16f12a19-0000-0000-0000-000000000000` when the real
value is `16f12a19-24be-4ed5-a53b-19b48f24e1e5` — the same first eight
characters, which is exactly the shape that reads as correct. The broker
answers `credential not found`, which is indistinguishable from a
credential that was never created (openregister#2245). Read them off
`GET /api/credentials`; never from memory.

🔴🔥 `onError` IS ON THE NODE, NOT IN `config`, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE
WHOLE FIX. `FlowEngine::outcomeForFailedStep()` reads `$step['onError']`,
and `FlowTokenRouter::stepFor()` returns the NODE — so the engine looks at
`node.onError` and never at `node.config.onError`. openconnector's
`SourceCallNode` reads `config.onError` ITSELF, which is why `read-dev-ref`
works with it there and why the wrong placement looks correct by example.
hermiq's workload node does not: it throws, and the engine's policy is the
only thing that decides.

⚠️ MEASURED, because it was written in `config` first and looked right.
A positive control pointed `ref` at a branch that does not exist:

    run-build  failed  repo checkout of "zz-no-such-ref…" failed (exit 128)
    (run stopped — dequeue, unlock and release never fired)

Identical to the behaviour the fix was supposed to remove. A `continue` in
the wrong half of the node is not a weaker policy, it is NO policy — and it
reads as one on the canvas, in the diff, and in review.

🔴 `onError` IS `continue` BECAUSE A REFUSAL HERE USED TO STRAND THE RUN.
Measured: the agent implemented the change and also edited `openapi.json`,
`pushGuard` correctly refused the push, and the refusal — which arrives as a
THROW, deliberately, so it can never be mistaken for a 200 carrying
`pushed: false` — killed the run at this node. The token stops here, so
`dequeue`, `unlock` and `release` never fire: the issue keeps `build:queued`,
the lock row survives, and the slot stays held. NOTHING IS RETRIED AND
NOTHING COMPLAINS.

⚠️ AND DO NOT COUNT ON THE LEASE TO CLEAN UP AFTER THIS. `claim-slot` sets
`leaseSeconds: 5400`, but the lease is a feature of `FlowStateNode` that
arrived with openregister#2486 — merged to `development`, and NOT
necessarily running. Checked on this instance while writing this: zero
occurrences of `leaseSeconds` in the deployed
`lib/Service/Flow/Nodes/FlowStateNode.php`, because the shared checkout sits
on a feature branch older than the merge. Where the lease is not deployed
the config key is inert and a stranded slot is held INDEFINITELY — the
original four-hour measurement, not a bounded ninety minutes. A recovery
mechanism that is merged is not a recovery mechanism that is running.

⚠️ EVERY node between `claim-slot` and `dequeue` has this exposure, and this
one is simply the one that fires — it runs a model for up to 25 minutes
against a network, so it is where a failure actually lands.

🔑 THE ABSENCE OF `build` IS THE DISCRIMINATOR, and it is the reason no
change to hermiq was needed. A run that SUCCEEDS always writes `build`, even
when the agent honestly changed nothing (`push.pushed: false`). A run that
THROWS — refused push, dead container, timeout — writes nothing at all,
because the engine leaves `$items` untouched when a `continue` step fails. So
`built-gate` can tell 'ran, nothing to do' from 'could not run' without
reading an error message, which is the distinction stage.js's push phase is
written to preserve.

🔑 `CHANGELOG.md` IS IN SCOPE FOR THE SAME REASON, AND THE FLEET ALREADY
ASKS FOR IT. Measured: **43 `tasks.md` files across the organisation name
`CHANGELOG.md` in their `**files**` list** — it is a routine co-change, not
an edge case. Leaving it out means an agent that does exactly what its own
tasks.md told it to do gets its push refused at the very end, after the full
model run, and the whole build is spent to produce a `build:blocked`.

⚠️ Like `openapi.json` it stays a NAMED file rather than a loosened rule.
Dependency manifests, workflow definitions and shared config remain refused
by `pushGuard` regardless of what any spec asks for.

🔑 `openapi.json` IS IN SCOPE BECAUSE IT IS COUPLED TO `appinfo/routes.php`.
A change that adds endpoints and does not describe them leaves the API
description lying about the API. This is not speculative widening: the
file-actions change's own history carries `5e6db44f1 file-actions: document
file endpoints in openapi.json`, so the fleet already treats it as part of
the work. It stays a NAMED file rather than a loosened rule — dependency
manifests, workflow definitions and shared config remain refused.

🔑 A BUILD THAT CHANGED NOTHING IS AN OUTCOME, AND WITHOUT THIS ROUTE IT
IS A CRASH. The agent's prompt says in as many words that changing
nothing is a real answer, and the runner agrees: an empty change set
returns `{pushed: false, commit: '', files: []}` and is explicitly not a
failure — 'a builder that found the work already done is a legitimate
outcome'.

But `run-stage` checks out `feature/<issue>/hydra-build`, and on that path
the branch was never created. So the honest answer arrived as a checkout
failure naming a ref, which reads as a broken push rather than as an agent
that had nothing to do — the pipeline would have punished exactly the
behaviour it asks for.

⚠️ The condition tests `pushed` and NOT the file count. They can disagree:
`pushGuard` refuses a push for reasons that have nothing to do with the
diff being empty (a branch outside the allowlist, a dependency manifest, a
path outside `scope`), and a refusal THROWS rather than returning false.
`pushed: false` therefore means one thing only.

🔴 THREE OUTCOMES, AND THE THIRD IS THE ABSENCE OF THE FIRST TWO. Because
`run-build` is now `onError: continue`, a refusal no longer kills the run —
it arrives HERE, and it must not be filed as `build:no-change`. The two are
opposite operational signals: 'the agent found the work already done' needs
nobody, while 'the agent did the work and the fence refused it' needs a
human to widen `scope` or re-scope the issue. Labelling both `no-change`
would bury the second in the first, silently, forever.

🔑 THE TEST IS FOR `json.build` ITSELF, not for an error field, and that is
what makes it reliable. The engine does not decorate the item when a
`continue` step fails — it leaves `$items` exactly as the step received
them — so there IS no `__error` to read at a workload node. What there is,
is a hole: `build` is written on every successful run and on no failed one.
An existence check is therefore the strongest available discriminator AND
the cheapest, and it covers refusals, timeouts and dead containers alike
without enumerating them.

⚠️ ORDER MATTERS. `pushed === true` must be tried first: `===` against an
absent var yields false rather than throwing, so a failed run would
otherwise fall into whichever rule ran first. Rule two then absorbs every
surviving success, and the default is reached ONLY by a run that produced
no output at all.

🔑 THE GATES JUDGE THE BRANCH THE BUILD PUSHED, NOT THE BRANCH IT STARTED FROM.

This node asked for `--scope-to-diff` and did not get it, for the whole of the
pipeline's life. It checked out `{{stageRef}}` — the repository's DEFAULT
branch — so the diff base resolved to HEAD, there was no push event to take a
previous tip from, and the runner fell back to a FULL-TREE AUDIT. Measured on
2026-08-13: `SCOPE-FILE-COUNT: 95`, `Scope: diff vs 4b825dc6…` — git's EMPTY
TREE. Three different planix issues about three different OpenSpec changes each
returned the identical nine gates, because all three audited the same 95 files.
The verdict was a property of the REPOSITORY and had nothing to do with the
issue it was stamped on (#544).

`run-build` now produces a branch with a commit on it, so there is finally a
real diff to scope to: this checks out that branch and names the base
explicitly. `--base` is passed rather than left to inference because inference
is exactly what failed before — the runner has four ways to guess a base and
each one degrades to the full tree, LOUDLY but non-fatally, which is how the
mis-scoping survived so long.

⚠️ `origin/` IS LOAD-BEARING. The stage clones and checks out the feature
branch, so the base branch exists only as a REMOTE-TRACKING ref in that clone.
A bare `{{stageRef}}` would not resolve, and the runner's fallback would send
it straight back to a full-tree audit — a green-looking run measuring the wrong
thing, which is the failure this change exists to end.

⚠️ The branch name is duplicated from `run-build`'s `push.branch` rather than
read from the stage result: the runner returns `push.branch`, but a template
that reads it would silently gate the DEFAULT branch if the push were ever
skipped, which is the same class of silent mis-scoping. Both halves are the
same literal, and `feature/{{issueNumber}}/hydra-build` is a pure function of
the issue — so if one is changed and the other is not, the checkout fails
outright instead of quietly auditing everything.

🔴 `onError` IS `continue` SO THAT A DEAD GATE RUN UNWINDS INSTEAD OF
STRANDING. On `stop` the token dies here holding the lock and the slot, and
the issue keeps `build:queued` with a branch already pushed — the worst of
the three states, because the code EXISTS and nothing points at it.
Downstream, `verdict-gate` reads the absence of `stage` and routes to
`build-blocked`, which is honest: the build is real, the verdict is not.

hydra's gate runner uses its exit code as a failure COUNT, so zero is the only pass. Routing on the number rather than on a verdict field is deliberate — nothing between the runner and here gets to reinterpret it. ⚠️ `===`, NOT `==`. FlowExpression is jwadhams/json-logic-php, whose `==` is PHP's loose `==`; this read `==` until 2026-08-02 and an ABSENT `exitCode` therefore evaluated `null == 0` → TRUE → `passed`. Measured live on the deployed instance. That is the entire defect this change exists to close, sitting in the router that actually gates every build: a stage whose output carried no exit code at all — a workload that never produced one — was routed as a clean gate run. `===` answers false for an absent key, for `"0"`, and for `false`.

🔴 AND THAT SAME ABSENT `exitCode` MUST NOT NOW BECOME A FIXER RUN. `===`
correctly answers false for it, but the old default sent everything that was
not a pass to `run-fix` — so once `run-stage` became `onError: continue`, a
gate run that DIED would have dispatched the fixer to repair findings nobody
measured. Twenty-five minutes of model time spent against an empty finding
list, ending in a PR labelled `build:fail` on the strength of no evidence.

🔑 SO THE PASS AND THE FAIL BOTH REQUIRE `stage` TO EXIST, and the default is
now the one case where it does not. Rule two is the honest fail — a real
verdict with a non-zero count, which is what the fixer is for. The default is
`verdict-blocked`: the branch is pushed and real, and the only thing missing
is an opinion about it.

🔴🔥 IT IS A SEPARATE NODE FROM `build-blocked`, AND THAT IS NOT DUPLICATION
— IT IS THE FIX FOR A SILENT ITEM LOSS. Both gates pointed at ONE
`build-blocked` node first, and the run measured this:

    built-gate     in 1 out 1   tagged the item `build-blocked`
    verdict-gate   in 0 out 0   fired as a heartbeat
    …
    build-blocked  in 0 out 0   THE ITEM WAS GONE

`FlowItemPlacement::advanceItems()` writes `placeItems[$to] =
itemsForOutput(...)` for every one of a firing node's outputs — an
ASSIGNMENT, not an append, and it runs whether the node produced items or
not. Every node in the graph fires on every pass, most of them with nothing,
so `verdict-gate`'s empty firing overwrote the place `built-gate` had just
filled. The consumer's turn came last and found an empty list.

🔑 THE RULE THAT FOLLOWS: two nodes may not write the same place when the
consumer fires between them. Convergence itself is fine — `dequeue` takes
three incoming edges and works, because the engine visits it immediately
after each predecessor. What is not fine is a place written by a node in
ANOTHER branch of the same pass.

⚠️ AND EVERY LAYER OF IT READ AS SUCCESS. The run reported `completed`. The
routing was perfect — the emitted item carried `output: "build-blocked"` and
no `build` key, exactly as designed. `build-blocked` fired and logged
`completed`. The only trace of the loss anywhere was the `in 0`.

The quality gates ran over the change you just made on this branch and found problems in it. Fix them.

You are in a checkout of `{{repo}}` at `feature/{{issueNumber}}/hydra-build` — the branch carrying your own commit, not the base. The findings below are about the files in that commit.

=== GATE OUTPUT ===
{{stage.output}}

Fix what the findings name, and nothing else. Do not refactor, do not rename, do not improve code the gates did not mention — a fixing pass that rewrites more than it was asked to makes the diff unreviewable and buries the original change.

Some findings may not be about your code. A gate that judges the repository's own configuration (a shared coding standard, a test matrix, a dependency policy) reports pre-existing debt that your commit did not introduce and cannot properly fix. Leave those alone and say which ones you left.

Do NOT run git. Edit the working tree and stop; the pipeline commits what you changed.

If a finding is wrong, or fixing it correctly would need a change outside this branch's scope, change nothing for that finding and say so. A gate count that stays non-zero for a stated reason is a better answer than a plausible edit that silences it.
config.$comment:
🔑 THE STEP THAT MAKES A BUILD CONVERGE. Everything before this produces
one attempt and a number; this reads the number back and acts on it. A
pipeline that only ever reports `exit=6` has told a person what to do —
it has not done it.

It clones the BRANCH, not the base. That is the difference from
`run-build`: the findings are about the commit that already exists, so
the agent has to be standing on it. Pushing back to the same branch is
then a fast-forward, and `pushGuard` accepts it under the same
`feature/<issue>/<slug>` rule as the first push.

🔑 ONE PASS, NOT A LOOP, and that is a deliberate bound rather than a
missing feature. A loop needs a counter, a cap, and somewhere to keep
them, and every one of those is a way to spend model time without
converging — the failure mode is not a crash, it is a bill. One pass
fixes the findings that are mechanically fixable (a missing @copyright,
a missing @spec, an absent auth attribute) which is most of what the
gates report, and anything still failing after it is exactly what a
person should be looking at.

⚠️ The prompt tells the agent to fix what the findings name AND NOTHING
ELSE. Without that a fixing pass rewrites more than it was asked to and
buries the original change in an unreviewable diff — the pull request
stops being about the issue.

⚠️ It is also told that some findings are not about its code. gate-65
judges the repository's own coding-standard adoption and fires on a
clean diff; asking an agent to 'fix' that invites it to edit shared
configuration to silence a gate, which is the worst possible response to
a finding.

A fixing pass that changed nothing goes straight to the verdict with the
FIRST gate result standing. Re-running the gates over a tree that did not
move would spend minutes to reproduce a number already held, and — worse —
would make an unchanged run look like a second opinion.

Tests `pushed` for the same reason `built-gate` does: `pushGuard` REFUSES
by throwing, so `false` here means one thing only — the agent decided
there was nothing it could correctly change.

The same gates, the same scope, over the fixed tree.

🔑 `output: "stage"` OVERWRITES the first result ON PURPOSE. Everything
downstream — `verdict-gate`, the label, the pull-request body — reads
`stage`, and what they should report is the state the branch is actually
in, not the state it was in before the fixing pass. Writing to a second
key would leave the verdict quietly describing a tree that no longer
exists.

⚠️ AND THE OVERWRITE IS WHY THIS NODE ALONE DOES NOT NEED A BLOCKED ROUTE.
Under `onError: continue` a failed re-gate writes nothing, so `stage` keeps
the PRE-FIX verdict — present, and non-zero, because a zero would never have
reached the fixer. `verdict-gate-2` therefore routes to `advance-failed`,
which opens the pull request and labels it `build:fail`.

🔑 THAT IS THE RIGHT FAILURE DIRECTION, and it is worth being explicit that
it is a stale number rather than a measured one. The alternative — routing a
dead re-gate to `build-blocked` — would throw away a branch that already
exists and already has fixes on it, because the SECOND opinion could not be
taken. Reporting the first opinion is conservative: it can only overstate the
remaining findings, never understate them, since the fixing pass runs between
the two.

The verdict after the fixing pass, and it reads the SAME `stage` key the
first one did — `run-regate` overwrote it. A build whose findings the
fixer cleared reaches `advance` and is labelled `build:pass`; one that
still has findings reaches `advance-failed`, with the pull request
carrying the SECOND gate output rather than the first.

🔑 THE LABEL IS THE LITERAL `build:pass`, RESOLVING AN AMBIGUITY THE PLACEHOLDER HID. This was `{{runLabel}}` — a name that says 'running' on an edge reachable only from the `passed` branch. hydra's state machine (scripts/create-labels.sh, CLAUDE.md) reads `build:queued -> build:running -> build:pass`, and the label that means 'gates passed' is `build:pass`; `build:running` is applied when a stage STARTS, which is not what this edge does. The graph's shape was right and the placeholder's name was wrong, and while it stayed unbound nothing forced anyone to notice. Labels are hydra CONVENTIONS rather than per-run values, so they are hardcoded at both ends of the machine — `scripts/create-labels.sh` creates exactly these strings and this flow uses exactly these strings. ⚠️ KNOWN GAP, stated rather than papered over: `scripts/lib/labels.sh` supports a `HYDRA_LABEL_PREFIX` (`wilco-build:queued`) applied by `_apply_prefix`, and a flow has no equivalent. An instance running prefixed labels must seed this flow with the prefixed literals. Making the label a placeholder is exactly the shape that made this flow dormant, so the gap is documented instead of reintroduced.
The FAIL label, and the slot is still released afterwards: a failed gate run is a completed tick, not a stuck one. Holding the slot would starve the pool over something that finished.

🔑 THE VERDICT IS NOT WHAT TAKES THE ISSUE OUT OF THE QUEUE — THIS IS. `advance` and `advance-failed` only ADD `build:pass` / `build:fail`; neither REMOVES `build:queued`, and `find-work` searches on exactly that label with `per_page: 1`. So without this node the next tick re-finds the same issue, and the one after that, forever: the queue has a head and no way to consume it. Measured on 2026-08-12 — run 56911 handled planix#248 to completion, and runs 56912 and 56913, the two ticks that followed, both died at `lock-issue` with `An object with identifier "zz-lock-planix-248" already exists.` The pipeline was not idle and was not broken; it was re-picking one issue it had already finished. NOTE that a verdict label and the queue label are different facts and both are wanted on the issue afterwards: `build:fail` says what happened, and the ABSENCE of `build:queued` says it is no longer waiting. ⚠️ `onError: continue`, not `stop`, and the asymmetry is deliberate. GitHub answers 404 when the label is not on the issue, which is the state this node is trying to reach — failing the run over an already-correct issue would strand the lock that `unlock` below is about to release. A label that cannot be removed for a real reason still shows up: the issue keeps `build:queued` and the next tick re-finds it, which is the same signal as before, unmissable.

The lock is RELEASED BY THE RUN THAT TOOK IT, rather than left for `hydra-lock-reaper` to age out. The reaper is a backstop for a run that died holding one, not the ordinary path: until it fires, an issue that has been built cannot be built again, and a retry arriving inside that window fails at `lock-issue` looking exactly like a genuine concurrent claim. `release` below frees the concurrency SLOT and is a different fact — the slot is about how many repositories may be in flight, the lock is about this one issue. ⚠️ `onNoMatch: "skip"`, because the reaper may legitimately have got there first; a lock that is already gone is the state this node wants and not an error. 🔑 `permanent: true`, AND THE DEFAULT WOULD BE WRONG HERE. A soft delete
leaves the row in place with `_deleted` set, and the magic table's `_uuid`
unique index carries NO `WHERE _deleted IS NULL` predicate — while its
sibling `..._live_owner_idx` does, which is what makes the omission visible
rather than a guess. So the tombstone goes on holding the identifier, and
the create path disagrees with it: `findAndValidateExistingObject()` looks
for a conflict with `includeDeleted: false`, finds nothing, and proceeds,
only for the write underneath to be refused.

That is survivable for a record, which is archived and never re-created
under the same identifier. It is fatal for a CLAIM. This lock's id is
deliberately a pure function of (repo, issue) — that is what makes two
concurrent ticks collide on it — so it cannot be varied per attempt without
giving up the mutual exclusion it exists for. A claim that cannot destroy
its own row can therefore be taken exactly ONCE, ever, and every retry of
that issue afterwards dies at `lock-issue` with `already exists` about a row
every read reports as absent.

Measured before the fix: `zz-lock-openregister-1561` was soft-deleted at
22:54 and still refused a fresh claim at 07:10 the next morning.

⚠️ Permanence is the RIGHT default for this node and the WRONG one for the
engine, which is why `openregister.object-write` still tombstones unless
asked. A lock is not a record: there is nothing to archive, nothing to
restore, and no audit question its corpse answers that the run log does not.
openregister#2467 added the flag behind the same guards as every other
delete — an explicit match, exactly one row, `confirmDelete`, and `permanent`
itself boolean-only.

All slots occupied. The tick ends without dispatching.

config.$comment:
🔑 A THIRD VERDICT, BECAUSE THERE ARE THREE OUTCOMES. `build:pass` and
`build:fail` are both claims about CODE THAT EXISTS. An agent that read
the spec, found the work already done or found it could not start, and
changed nothing has produced neither — and labelling that `build:fail`
would say the gates rejected work that was never written.

That distinction is not cosmetic: it is what a person deciding what to do
next needs. `build:fail` means read the diff; `build:no-change` means read
the issue, because either the spec is already satisfied or it does not say
enough to act on.

⚠️ NEW VOCABULARY. `scripts/create-labels.sh` does not create this one, and
GitHub auto-creates a label on first use — which is how the fleet ended up
with a grey undescribed `build:fail` beside a curated `build:failed`. Add
it to that script rather than leaving it to the API's default.

🔴 A FOURTH VERDICT, AND IT EXISTS BECAUSE A RUN THAT COULD NOT FINISH USED
TO LEAVE NO TRACE AT ALL. Measured on 2026-08-14: the agent implemented
openregister#1549 correctly and also edited `openapi.json`, which was
outside the declared `scope`. `pushGuard` refused — correctly — and the
refusal ended the run at `run-build`. The issue kept `build:queued`, the
lock row survived, the slot stayed held, and the only record anywhere was
one line in a flow-run log. (`claim-slot` asks for a 5400-second lease, but
that is openregister#2486 and it is merged, not necessarily DEPLOYED —
checked here and absent — so do not assume the slot comes back on its own.)

🔑 THIS IS NOT `build:fail` AND IT IS NOT `build:no-change`. All three say
'no pull request', which is exactly why they get confused, and they ask a
person for three different things:

  build:fail       code exists, gates judged it, findings remain
                   → read the diff
  build:no-change  the agent ran and honestly changed nothing
                   → read the issue; the spec is satisfied or too thin
  build:blocked    the agent could not complete, or a fence stopped it
                   → read the RUN; hydra itself is what needs changing

Only the third is a statement about the PIPELINE rather than about the
work, and collapsing it into either of the others hides the one class of
failure that nobody else will find.

⚠️ THE REASON IS NOT ON THE ISSUE, and that is a real limitation rather
than an oversight. A step that fails under `onError: continue` contributes
nothing to the item — the engine leaves `$items` untouched — so the refusal
message exists only in the run log. The label says WHERE to look; it cannot
say what happened. Carrying the reason would mean hermiq returning a
refusal as data, which `stage.js` deliberately refuses to do so that a
refused push can never be read as a 200.

⚠️ Like `build:no-change`, this leans on GitHub auto-creating an unknown
label on first use. `scripts/create-labels.sh` defines the curated version
with a colour and a description; without it the fleet accumulates grey
undescribed duplicates.

🔑 `verdict-blocked` IS THE SAME NODE FOR THE OTHER GATE, and the two are
not merged into one on purpose. See the note on `verdict-gate`: a place
written by two nodes in different branches of the same pass loses its items
to whichever writes last, because `advanceItems()` ASSIGNS rather than
appends and every node fires each pass whether it has work or not. Sharing
this node cost exactly one run, silently, with `completed` on the tin.

The same verdict as `build-blocked` — `build:blocked`, meaning hydra could
not finish and the RUN is what needs reading — reached from the other gate.

🔴 IT IS A SECOND NODE BECAUSE ONE SHARED NODE SILENTLY ATE THE ITEM. Both
gates named `build-blocked` at first, and the measured run went:

    built-gate     in 1 out 1   item tagged `build-blocked`
    verdict-gate   in 0 out 0   heartbeat, in another branch
    build-blocked  in 0 out 0   nothing arrived

`FlowItemPlacement::advanceItems()` sets `placeItems[$to]` for each of a
firing node's outputs. It is an assignment, and it happens on every firing
including the empty ones — so a node that shares an output place with a
branch that fires later, but before the consumer, has its items replaced
with an empty list. The run still reported `completed`.

🔑 CONVERGENCE IS NOT THE PROBLEM; ORDER IS. `dequeue` has three incoming
edges and works, because the engine visits it directly after each
predecessor. The rule to keep is narrower than 'avoid shared targets': do
not let two branches of the same pass write one place with the consumer
scheduled between them. When in doubt, give the branch its own node — a
duplicated four-line source-call is cheap, and losing an item is not.

✅ THE ENGINE DEFECT ITSELF IS FIXED (openregister#2489): a firing that
produced no items now places nothing and destroys nothing, so a shared place
survives a heartbeat. Verified on the running instance by deliberately
restoring the shared node — `built-gate in 1`, `verdict-gate in 0`,
`build-blocked in 1`.

⚠️ THE SPLIT STAYS ANYWAY, and it is not superstition. A flow definition is
portable and an engine version is not: this same JSON is seeded onto
instances whose OpenRegister predates the fix, where the shared place still
loses the item — silently, with `completed` on the run. Keeping one writer
per place costs four lines and is correct on every engine. Do not collapse
these two nodes back together as a tidy-up.

config.$comment:
THE GENERIC STAGE AGENT. One node serves code review, security review
and the applier — the difference is `persona`, set by the cascade, and
the brief the agent reads out of the tool tree.

🔑 `async: true` IS WHAT MAKES A SLOT MEAN SOMETHING. The stage is
STARTED and a handle comes back; the run then suspends on `review-wait`,
which releases the queue worker. `FlowRunWorker` advances runs serially
in one process, so a synchronous stage would hold the only worker for
the whole review and the pool could never exceed one agent however many
slots it declared.

⚠️ NO `push`. A reviewer's bounded fixes are committed by its own brief
through the forge API, not by `pushGuard` — this stage is not a builder
and must not be handed a writing posture it was not designed for.

🔑 `collect` NAMES THE VERDICT FILE because the stage's filesystem is
deleted moments after it ends. A review whose answer lived only in the
clone is a review nobody can act on — the same gap `create_finding_issues`
hit before the runner could return files.

SUSPENDS the run. The engine stores the marking and the items, frees
the worker, and wakes this run when `resumeAt` is due — which is the
entire mechanism by which four slots become four agents rather than a
queue of one.

⚠️ The node runs a SECOND time on the way back in and lets the items
straight through, because the marking is not advanced while suspended.
That is what makes it correct rather than a one-shot.
Asks what became of the handle. A `done` result is published as `stage`, in the SAME shape a synchronous step produces, so the verdict gate cannot tell which transport delivered it.

🔴🔥 THE 'STILL RUNNING' EXIT PARKS THE RUN — IT DOES NOT LOOP BACK.

It looped back to `review-wait` first, and the engine stopped it:

    Flow did not settle within 1000 transitions; it may contain an
    unbounded loop.

`WaitNode` suspends on its FIRST pass and, on the way back in, sees
`context.resuming` and lets the items straight through — which is what
makes resume correct, and what makes it useless as a loop body. The
second arrival did not suspend, so wait → collect → wait spun at full
speed until the ceiling caught it. The ceiling did its job; the loop was
the mistake, and its own node comment had described the pass-through
behaviour it then depended on NOT happening.

🔑 SO THE RUN ENDS AND A LATER TICK COLLECTS — which is the same rule
the rest of this flow already follows: nothing is handed forward, the
next tick re-reads state and picks up whatever is there. The handle is
parked on the lock object so a later tick can find it.

  running  park the handle, end the run, free the slot's worker
  done     the stage RAN; a non-zero exit is a verdict
  default  failed / unknown — both TERMINAL

THE VERDICT IS THE FILE, NOT THE EXIT CODE.

A reviewer that crashed, ran out of turns, or answered in prose exits
0 just as readily as one that reviewed. `hydra-verdict.json` is the
only artefact that distinguishes them, which is why the dispatch
`collect`s it by name and why an absent file resolves to `missing`
rather than to a pass.

🔑 `ranGates` IS `_verify_reviewer_ran_mandatory_gates`, PORTED. The
orchestrator audit lists it as one of two capabilities that must not
be dropped silently, precisely because it guards a GREEN-BUT-DEAD
review: an agent that skips the mechanical gates and reports `pass`
is indistinguishable from one that ran them, unless something asks.
This asks, on the reviewer's own declaration of what it ran.

🔴 THE ALIAS, NOT THE FILENAME. This read `stage.files.hydra-verdict.json`,
and a flow addresses data with a DOTTED path — so that key splits at every
dot and resolves to nothing, whatever the runner returned. The runner's own
collect code carries the warning: an array keys each file by its own path,
and `collect: {verdict: "hydra-verdict.json"}` is the form a flow can walk.

The file never arrived either: the flow declared `collect`, the node dropped
it, and `buildParams()` never put it on the wire. So EVERY review hydra has
run read `missing` and was blocked — a correct refusal for a reason that was
never true.

🔴🔥 `fromJson` DESTROYED THE VERDICT, and did it silently.

The runner PARSES a collected `.json` file before returning it — deliberately,
because a flow cannot address into a string. So `stage.files.verdict` arrives
as an OBJECT, and `fromJson` on an object returns NULL. Measured directly
against the engine: fromJson(object) -> null, fromJson(string) -> the object,
var(object) -> the object.

Every review therefore read `verdict: missing`, `ranGates: false`, and was
blocked — while the reviewer had written a perfect verdict file declaring
`checks_run: ["hydra-gates", ...]`. THREE layers were blamed before the
expression: the agent (which had run the gates and said so), the prompt (which
named the file but not the array), and the brief (which was already emphatic).
None of them was wrong.

⚠️ The false trail was my own probe. Grepping the run log for
`"verdict":"pass"` matched the string INSIDE the collected file, not the
computed field — so the compute looked like it had worked.

A review that did not run the gates is NOT a review, whatever it
concluded. It is refused here rather than recorded as a verdict —
the whole point of the guard is that a skipped check must not be able
to produce a pass.

⚠️ This refuses on the reviewer's OWN `checks_run` list. That is a
declaration, not proof, and a determined agent could lie — which is
why `scripts/verify-reviewer-gates.py` parses the JSONL transcript
instead. This is the cheap half; the transcript check is the honest
one and is still to be wired.
`missing` and anything else fall to blocked — an unreadable verdict is not a fail, it is a stage nobody can act on, and it needs a person rather than a label that looks like a judgement.
The verdict, on the issue. The NEXT tick reads it and dispatches whatever is now highest-priority — nothing is handed forward.
A failing review still advances the pipeline — the next stage is queued by the label machine, and a human reads the findings on the PR. Only `needs-input` stops.

`_analyze_verdicts`, PORTED — the other capability the orchestrator
audit says must not be dropped.

An issue carrying BOTH `<stage>:pass` and `<stage>:fail` is a
reviewer-dispatch race, and it is not a cosmetic mess: every later
gate that reads 'did this pass' gets a different answer depending on
which label it looks at first. The audit's rule is FAIL TAKES

removed immediately after.

404, and that is the ordinary case rather than a problem.

The slot stays held until the collect resolves, so ignoring in-flight work
would also mean the pool never frees.

to something — the node reported `completed in 1 out 1` — and matched
nothing, which is indistinguishable from an empty queue: the tick fell
straight through to the review tier and dispatched a SECOND agent for an
issue that already had one running. The numeric form was verified through

Something in flight? Collect it. Otherwise fall through to the queues — a tick always does exactly one thing.

A marker cannot outlive what it refers to, so nothing here needs reaping.
